newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers' strike threatens lovers' roses.
newsitem.headline: French truckers' strike threatens lovers' roses.

text.p: French lovers risk a blighted Valentine's Day next February if a truckers' strike continues to throttle the nation's roads and fuel supplies.
Red rose growers in the south of France said on Thursday that lack of fuel for heating greenhouses could prevent the plants from flowering for Valentine's Day -- February 14, 1997.
"If we can't heat now, the entire Saint Valentine's production risks being affected," said Vincent Martel, a rose grower in Roquebrune-sur-Argens, inland from the Riviera coast.

Below 10 degrees Celsius (50 fahrenheit), roses fail to bloom. Martel said he had three days' reserves of gas supplies left to heat his plants. Overnight temperatures in the region have been close to freezing.
Valentine's Day represents about 15 percent of flower sales from the southeastern Var region, which produces between 50 and 60 percent of all France's cut flowers.
The region has 450 hectares (1,110 acres) of plants under glass, dependent on oil and gas supplies by truck, with an annual turnover of 800 million francs ($160 million).
Truckers kept up some 250 roadblocks on Thursday after talks to end their 11-day-old strike broke down.

Bruno Bury, a producer of poinsettias, a red-leaved tropical plant known as "Christmas stars" in France and sold to brighten homes in winter, said he had cut temperatures in his greenhouses to 14 C (57C) from 18C (64F) to conserve fuel.
"One night without heating and it's screwed up. Good for the rubbish bin," he said. Bury's poinsettias are sold throughout eastern France and Switzerland.

"I'm going to run out (of fuel) tomorrow morning," he said. He added "I've got a small reserve at home, I'll decant it to try to gain half a day." He said he ordered fuel last week but it had yet to arrive because of truckers' road blockades.
His 80,000 poinsettias are worth an estimated nine million francs ($1.75 million), and his firm employs 45 people.
The strike, especially targeting fuel supplies, has led to petrol rationing for many motorists, closed factories for lack of spare parts and clogged ports with foreign trucks.
Some flower producers are slashing prices or even destroying their blooms.
Martel said he sold most of his roses at the Rungis market in the southern Paris suburbs. The news on Thursday was encouraging -- a truck that left on Wednesday had arrived.
Bury's trucks are all blocked. He said local authorities should requisition fuel to safeguard the flower producers.
Martel worried that the strike, over truckers' demands for higher pay, shorter hours and retirement at 55 instead of 60, could lead to higher transport costs that would knock on to suppliers.
"Companies like ours that are already facing problems will be forced under," he said.
